lessons.title: the sounds of shona
lessons.description: i can recognize the vowels and key consonant clusters of shona
lessons.skillOutcome: i can recognize the vowels and key consonant clusters of shona
learningObjectives: gain skill: i can recognize the vowels and key consonant clusters of shona
culturalNotes: shona has five pure vowels — a, e, i, o, u — that never glide. they stay steady on one quality.
the consonant clusters "mh" and "nh" are voiced and have low pitch — they sound heavier than english "m" or "n" alone.

vocabulary.usageNote: modern equivalent to FSI mangwanani/masikati for informal contexts

lessons.description: i can count from one to five in shona
lessons.skillOutcome: i can count from one to five in shona
learningObjectives: gain skill: i can count from one to five in shona
culturalNotes: shona numbers have two forms: counting words ("posi, piri, tatu, china, shanu") and concord stems ("-mwe, -viri, -tatu, -na, -shanu") that attach to noun-class prefixes.
so "two children" is "vana va-viri" — the va- agrees with class 2.

learningObjectives: gain skill: i can explain how unhu (humanness) shapes shona speech
culturalNotes: unhu (also known as ubuntu in nguni languages) means "i am because we are". it explains why shona greetings are slow, why family terms extend to strangers, and why the plural is used for respect.
when you take time to greet someone — and ask about their family, their children, their journey — you are practicing unhu.

lessons.title: the totem tradition — mutupo
lessons.description: i can recognize totem-names and their role in shona identity
lessons.skillOutcome: i can recognize totem-names and their role in shona identity
learningObjectives: gain skill: i can recognize totem-names and their role in shona identity
culturalNotes: every shona family belongs to a totem (mutupo) — usually an animal, like shumba (lion), soko (monkey), or moyo (heart). people of the same totem are considered relatives.
in fsi practice texts, "Baba naMai Shumba" — "Mr. and Mrs. Shumba" — appear repeatedly. "Shumba" is a totem-derived surname.

lessons.title: tsuro naDiro — a folktale
lessons.description: i can follow a simple shona folktale and pick out its message
lessons.skillOutcome: i can follow a simple shona folktale and pick out its message
learningObjectives: gain skill: i can follow a simple shona folktale and pick out its message
culturalNotes: fsi unit 41 contains the folktale "tsuro naDiro" — the hare and Diro. the hare convinces Diro to dig up sweet potatoes alone while he "keeps watch". the lesson: cleverness without ethics ends badly (Diro is caught by the farmers and pays the price).
"tsumo" — proverbs — carry these moral lessons in compressed form. shona stories and proverbs are the original "language curriculum" of the culture.
